title: Admin UI looks dated and is hard to navigate
summary: The most repeated usability complaint across engines: the management console looks old, functions are scattered, and large environments are hard to manage from it. Cloverleaf users went as far as unofficial icon patches to make the Java IDE legible.
quote: the UI is somewhat outdated, making it difficult to manage with large environments

title: Steep learning curve; productive use needs specialist training
summary: Reviewers say new staff struggle for months: setup is heavy, concepts (productions, globals, Xlates, lockers) are engine-specific, and legacy and modern patterns coexist. Corepoint is cited as easier than Rhapsody; Cloverleaf and InterSystems as hardest.
quote: Corepoint definitely had an easier user interface than Rhapsody.

title: Proprietary scripting language (ObjectScript, Tcl, Lua) shrinks the hiring pool
summary: Engines built on niche languages force teams to hire or train scarce specialists; reviewers compare them unfavourably with JavaScript-based engines. Iguana users also regretted the move from Python to Lua and say Lua mastery takes well over a year.
quote: Understanding ObjectScript isn't something everyone has

title: Licence and subscription cost is high relative to alternatives
summary: Cost is the most common value complaint in KLAS and review sites: commercial engines are described as among the most expensive line items, with costs that scale by cores, connections and modules, and some customers are going to market purely on price.
quote: Corepoint is one of our most expensive things.

title: Unpredictable renewals and maintenance-fee increases
summary: Customers report sizeable maintenance-fee jumps at renewal, annual true-ups of connections that surprise them, a post-COVID price increase from InterSystems, and Redox quotes that changed depending on who presented them.
quote: We have had some issues with the increases in Rhapsody's maintenance fees.

title: Essential capabilities sold as separately licensed modules
summary: Web services/API handling, extra adapters, SSL management and clustering are add-ons rather than core. Reviewers dislike discovering they must buy a module to call an API or that features are 'not out of the box'.
quote: In order to handle API calls, we need to purchase the web services module

title: Per-interface or per-connection pricing penalises trivial jobs
summary: Interface-count licensing means simple jobs such as scheduled SFTP pulls consume paid interface licences; Redox charged per connection and customers fear per-click charges. Mirth's 'unlimited channels per server' is marketed as the counterpoint.
quote: use a lot of interface licensing just to schedule SFTP file transfers

title: Mirth Connect moved from open source to closed commercial licence
summary: From 4.6 (March 2025) Mirth is proprietary and licence-only; source is no longer public and pricing is not published. Users and commentators call it a big change, spawning forks (Open Integration Engine, BridgeLink).
quote: went from being open source to a closed system

title: Last open-source Mirth versions get no security patches
summary: Sites that stay on 4.5.2 or earlier to avoid licensing are left without vendor security fixes, which commentators flag as a compliance risk for PHI-handling systems.

title: Vendor lock-in through proprietary configuration formats
summary: Channel/route definitions are opaque proprietary formats, so leaving means rebuilding every interface; integration networks tie you to their data model and roadmap; cloud FHIR stores tie you to one provider. Commentators note proprietary configs are also opaque to AI tooling.

title: Interface definitions are hard to put under version control
summary: Mirth stores channels in the database; InterSystems productions are one monolithic class and business rules lack source control; Cloverleaf is said to have no version control; Corepoint's is 'fiddly'; Iguana's Git integration is single-branch. Users want built-in change history (e.g. for DTLs) and Git-native workflows.
quote: integration with Git is single-branch based

title: Configuration only possible through the GUI; coders want config-as-code
summary: Most configuration requires clicking through a GUI, which frustrates developers who want scripted, reviewable, text-based configuration. Lightweight competitors pitch version-controllable rule files as a differentiator.
quote: Corepoint does what it needs to do, but I am a coder by trade

title: Promoting a batch of changes between environments is painful
summary: Users cannot easily package and apply only the changed parts of a production, BizTalk deployments need manual steps for hosted services and are hard to update, and InterSystems users want a UI to transfer projects between instances.
quote: Not easy to do a group of changes to be applied at same time

title: Deploying a change causes downtime or service recycle
summary: BizTalk reviewers report deployments require recycling the server, blocking users, and that updating solutions is a headache; they want faster, non-disruptive deploys.
quote: Updating things in BizTalk is a headache.

title: Built-in isolated dev/test/prod environments with staged promotion
summary: Vendors attack rivals for lacking sandbox testing, change control and staged deployment, indicating buyers weigh it heavily. Rhapsody and InterSystems market it as a strength; Mirth and Cloverleaf are portrayed as lacking it.

title: Visible per-environment colour banner to prevent production mistakes
summary: Third most-voted InterSystems idea (21 votes, planned): show a coloured banner identifying dev/test/prod so admins don't act on the wrong system.

title: Dark mode for the management portal
summary: Top-voted InterSystems idea (55 votes, planned) is a dark theme for the Management Portal.

title: Thick-client desktop IDE must be installed and kept in version lockstep
summary: Rhapsody's Windows IDE is not browser-based and must match the engine version; Cloverleaf's Tk/Java GUI pieces were dropped in 6.0, breaking customisations. Users want a browser-based admin that needs no client install.
quote: IDE developer windows application is pretty old still and isn't browser based

title: Forced IDE migration (Studio to VS Code) unpopular
summary: InterSystems deprecated Studio for VS Code; some teams hate the new IDE, and VS Code lacks the Inspector and legacy BPL/DTL editor integration. Others call Studio itself very poor, so neither option satisfies.
quote: My team universally hates the new IDE InterSystems is pushing.

title: Message search is slow and awkward
summary: Searching stored messages is a persistent pain: Health Connect users call it an ongoing challenge, Mirth databases bloat until queries crawl, and Redox users ask for Elastic/Kibana-style full-text search. InterSystems users also want export of search results and a refresh button.
quote: Message searching in the solution's database continues to be a challenge.

title: Message viewer only renders XML; want JSON and native views
summary: Interoperability message viewer defaults to XML; users requested a JSON display (two separate ideas), which the community had to build.

title: Resend/reprocess is coarse: can't target one destination or bulk resend
summary: Resending a message re-routes it to every original destination instead of only the failed operation; the viewer is unsuitable for resending more than ~100 messages; users ask to abort a specific message and to resend from the visual trace.

title: Purge should keep failed messages so they can be resent
summary: Second most-voted InterSystems idea (26 votes): add a purge filter that excludes errored messages so they survive retention and remain resendable.

title: Message store growth, pruning and archiving are manual burdens
summary: Without careful pruning the message database bloats and slows the whole engine; users want alerts on rapid DB growth, regex/wildcard archive rules for Message Bank, and better tracking/archiving for EDI.

title: Throughput ceiling at very high message volumes
summary: Mirth reviewers say it fits small-to-medium hospitals but struggled at millions of messages/day (one team built their own), is slower than wanted, and custom metadata hurts performance. Iguana users want better multi-core use; BizTalk HL7 is claimed to top out at a few hundred msg/s.
quote: we had issues talking about millions of messages per day

title: Per-message database writes force a trade-off between speed and audit trail
summary: The vendor's own tuning advice is to lower message storage because DB writes per message cap throughput; default full storage is called devastating for production performance, so teams sacrifice history for speed.

title: Heavy JVM/app-server footprint
summary: Engines are monolithic Java applications needing 1-2 GB heap; challengers contrast this with single-binary, ~128 MB, container-friendly designs. A 32-bit Mirth install also hit memory limits at a national lab.

title: High availability needs paid add-ons or manual clustering, and is buggy
summary: Mirth HA requires manual clustering or the paid Advanced Clustering extension; Rhapsody's Assured Availability is reported buggy; Cloverleaf relies on warm standby; Iguana users want load-balancing across two servers.
quote: Technically, Rhapsody has a redundant platform called Assured Availability, and it has been buggy.

title: Management service is a single point of failure
summary: A customer reported the main configuration service on the production server going down, causing an outage with slow vendor resolution.

title: DICOM adapter not usable in mirrored (HA) configuration
summary: Idea with 25 votes asks that the DICOM interoperability adapter work in a mirror/failover environment; status future consideration.

title: No native multi-tenancy; one instance per facility
summary: Large networks run separate servers per facility or environment because each instance is single-tenant. Rhapsody's 'lockers' (many hospitals in one instance) are cited as the model to copy.
quote: each instance is single-tenant

title: Monitoring shows the server is up, not whether channels are healthy
summary: Users want an at-a-glance web dashboard of channel/interface health, queue depth and errors. Mirth monitoring only confirms it is running; Health Connect monitoring 'could look better'; BizTalk needs third-party BizTalk360; Redox dashboards and Qvera metrics are thin.
quote: I cannot check the data inside Mirth Connect, such as the channels

title: Alerting is inflexible; want on-call routing and email/pager escalation
summary: Corepoint users dislike the current alert system, Health Connect users want the vendor to handle alert call routing, and BizTalk admins ask for basic email alerts on issues.
quote: I'm not a fan of the alert system as it currently stands in Corepoint.

title: Content-based alerts on clinical data (e.g. specific test code, missing field)
summary: Praised competitor capability: Corepoint Action Points notify people when a message contains a given result code or is missing data, configured by rule rather than code. Note: praised in competitor.

title: Basic ops features left to third-party or community add-ons
summary: Admins rely on external tools for everyday operations: BizTalk360 for monitoring, community packages (e.g. IRIS WHIZ) for queue search/sort, export of search results and viewer refresh, and community viewers for message browsing.

title: Queue visibility: search, sort and communicate delays
summary: Users ask for search and sort in the production queue panel, and for proactive notice of delays and backed-up queues because delays are costly.

title: Manage many engine instances from one console
summary: Users want to query and monitor several instances from one place; InterSystems users requested multi-instance querying and a read-only operations cockpit, while Mirth gates its central Command Center behind the enterprise licence.

title: Engine logs are poorly stored and hard to browse
summary: Iguana reviewers dislike how logs are stored, say the logs UI was better in an older version and the new one is slow; IRIS users want older message.log files viewable in the portal.
quote: the way it stores logs

title: Interface-level reporting and traffic analytics
summary: Users want built-in reports and analytics from message logs (traffic patterns, volumes, per-interface metrics); Redox lacks interface reporting, Iguana reporting needs customisation, Qvera could do more metrics, HealthShare custom reports are unwieldy.
quote: The only real downside is a lack of interface reporting.

title: Complete visual trace of a message across every component
summary: Health Connect reviewers repeatedly praise Visual Trace and complete message tracing as their favourite troubleshooting feature. Note: praised in competitor.
quote: The message trace is complete

title: AI analysis of errors and logs to prevent incidents
summary: Ideas ask for AI analysis of error logs and AI in the instance monitor to catch incidents early; KLAS respondents say InterSystems was late to AI and want it in Health Connect.

title: AI-assisted mapping and transformation generation from specs
summary: Rhapsody's AI mapping assistant is cited as a strength; InterSystems users request AI generation of transformations from interface specs and official AI access to DTL pages to cut drag-and-drop work. Some Corepoint users feel AI focus came at the expense of other development.

title: Expose the engine to AI agents (MCP, LLM observability)
summary: Recent ideas ask for MCP data-exposure toolkits, agent test UIs and LLM/agent observability dashboards; Rhapsody markets 'agent-ready interoperability'.

title: AI plus cloud may make heavyweight engines unnecessary
summary: A Corepoint analyst openly questions why they shouldn't use AI and the cloud to build what the engine does themselves, signalling loyalty risk for incumbents.
quote: what's to stop me from going to the cloud

title: Low-code visual mapping that analysts (not just programmers) can use
summary: Drag-and-drop DTLs (Health Connect) and Corepoint's ease of use are top praise; Iguana users want more drag-and-drop; Mirth's JavaScript-first model is called harder for non-programmers. Many interface analysts are not career coders.

title: Script sandbox gives poor access to engine internals
summary: A Mirth user says the JavaScript layer doesn't expose variables or class internals well, limiting customisation; another notes advanced work requires JavaScript knowledge.
quote: does not give me good access to the variables

title: Thin standard function libraries in the scripting layer
summary: Iguana users must write their own helpers due to few built-in Lua functions; IRIS users lack maths libraries and hand-build formulas; users also request time-zone conversion helpers.
quote: lack of in-built Lua functions

title: First-class mainstream language support (Python) still clunky
summary: Embedded Python is described as clunky; customers note the vendor says it will move toward Python; PyProd ideas ask for scaffolding CLI, templates and UI editing.
quote: Python support can be enhanced further, as it's really clunky at the moment

title: Only live runtime testing; want sandbox test harness and test data generators
summary: Cloverleaf is attacked for offering only live runtime testing; InterSystems users ask for HL7 test message generators, built-in test data generation and test dashboards.

title: Test-driven script editor that annotates code with live sample-message values
summary: Iguana's Translator (real-time, test-driven editing with annotations and sample data) is its signature praised feature and the reason users say they build interfaces much faster. Note: praised in competitor.

title: Fast inner loop: live reload and local debugging of components
summary: Ideas request a dev mode with live reload, local testing and debugging for production components, and an Embedded Python debugger in VS Code (implemented).

title: Documentation is thin, dense or hard to navigate
summary: Cloverleaf users want more documentation of features and new functionality; Health Connect docs are dense, fragmented and short on practical examples; IRIS method docs are sometimes missing; Corepoint's backend model is poorly documented; Redox implementation docs were generic.
quote: documentation can sometimes be dense or fragmented

title: Vendor training is declining, costly or self-serve only
summary: Very frequent KLAS theme: no more in-person courses, lacklustre or overwhelming online training, expensive extra seats, training outsourced to integrators, and no training bundled to cover staff turnover.
quote: Rhapsody's training has gotten a little lackluster lately.

title: Support and account relationship eroded after acquisitions
summary: Customers report account-manager churn, less outreach, reliance on third-party support, smaller customers being ignored, and paid premium plans that didn't deliver direct support.
quote: It seems like every few months, we get a new Rhapsody account manager

title: Innovation and release cadence slowed; product feels unchanged
summary: Corepoint customers see fewer releases since Rhapsody bought it; Cloverleaf is described as largely unchanged for years; BizTalk is seen as no longer evolving; Mirth users want NextGen to focus on its core.
quote: coming out with as many versions as they used to

title: Community and feedback channels weakened; no suggestion box or roadmap visibility
summary: Corepoint users say the user community and vendor requests for feedback have faded and want a suggestion box; Health Connect users lack visibility into the roadmap. InterSystems' public ideas portal (22% of ideas implemented) is a contrast.
quote: The community that we once felt among Corepoint users was stronger before.

title: Fast, knowledgeable human support
summary: The single most praised attribute across engines is support: Qvera responds within ~30 minutes, InterSystems WRC and Corepoint support are lauded, and Redox engineers were called incredibly responsive. Note: praised in competitors.

title: Vendor pushes its own cloud when customers want on-prem
summary: Cloverleaf customers say Infor pushes a cloud version they don't want and cloud migration is costly; Health Connect customers see more product moving to the vendor cloud.

title: No managed cloud option, or cloud-only with no on-prem option
summary: Mirth users say NextGen is behind on cloud and they still install everything; Iguana users want hosted options for small/mid sites; Redox users want an on-prem option. Buyers want both deployment models from one product.
quote: I think NextGen Healthcare is a little behind with cloud solutions.

title: Upgrades are hard, so customers fall versions behind
summary: Mirth upgrades are 'not as easy as hoped'; Corepoint sites run several versions behind and on unsupported servers; Iguana's own CEO says in-place upgrades to Iguana X ignored reality; Cloverleaf 6.0 removed Tk; IRIS mixes deprecated and new patterns.
quote: it's not as easy as I would hope it would be

title: Automated migration from another engine instead of rebuilding interfaces
summary: Switching engines means rebuilding every channel; vendors now compete on migration tooling (Rhapsody Auto Migrate from Cloverleaf, InterSystems Mirth migration services, Iguana 6-to-X converter), showing buyers value it.

title: Platform end-of-life forces costly migrations
summary: BizTalk is seen as a dead end with support ending (2016 and 2020 versions), pushing healthcare users to re-platform; Azure API for FHIR retirement forces moves to Health Data Services.
quote: BizTalk is in the past, Microsoft is not going to evolve it any further

title: Installation and initial setup are complex, especially on Linux
summary: Mirth install is harder on Linux than Windows; Health Connect installation is called more complex than it should be, lengthy and resource-intensive; Iguana on Linux/Mac only supports manual upgrade.
quote: Installing it on Linux is a bit harder

title: Marketplace images restrict instance sizes
summary: An AWS Marketplace Mirth image reportedly did not support EC2 instances larger than m5.xlarge, blocking vertical scaling.
quote: does not support EC2 Larger then M5.xlarge

title: Heavy on-prem infrastructure (servers plus SQL databases), no native cloud
summary: BizTalk needs physical servers and SQL databases and lacks native cloud support, requiring third-party adapters; on-prem Cloverleaf needs more servers as scale grows.
quote: BizTalk lacks native cloud support.

title: Small, Kubernetes-native engine with JSON logs, health probes and versioned rules
summary: New entrants pitch a single binary with no JVM, env-var config, structured logs, TCP health probes, graceful shutdown and version-controlled validation rules as the antidote to heavyweight engines.

title: Web service / REST integration harder than HL7
summary: Cloverleaf users say web-service integration could be easier; Corepoint requires a separately bought web services module; Redox doesn't support the full range of vendor APIs (e.g. SMART on FHIR).

title: File/SFTP transfer handling is weak
summary: Health Connect's FTP/SFTP architecture is called not ideal; Corepoint sites burn interface licences just to schedule SFTP transfers.
quote: Health Connect's FTP and SFTP architecture is not ideal.

title: Custom database connectivity is limited
summary: Corepoint customers want more capability for working with custom databases.
quote: Custom databases are an area where we'd like more capability in Corepoint.

title: OAuth2 support for HTTP adapters
summary: Users requested OAuth2 on outbound/inbound HTTP adapters (now implemented), reflecting modern API auth needs in healthcare integrations.

title: Cloud health platforms lack a native MLLP listener
summary: Azure MLLP support is preview/hybrid-only; Google needs a separately deployed MLLP adapter on GKE; HealthLake accepts only FHIR and needs custom Camel/Lambda pipelines or partners for HL7v2. A real engine is still required in front.

title: Cloud FHIR stores are data stores, not routing/transformation engines
summary: Comparisons stress that cloud health services store data but don't route, filter or transform; HL7v2-to-FHIR conversion relies on partner tools (e.g. InterSystems FHIR Transformation Service) or self-built code.

title: Cloud healthcare APIs require significant expertise to set up
summary: G2 reviewers say setup complexity is a barrier and integrating with existing hospital systems needs substantial technical resources.

title: FHIR support bolted on, partial, or not native
summary: Mirth is portrayed as HL7-first with FHIR as a plugin and reliant on community plugins for new standards; Redox users wanted native FHIR and SMART on FHIR; IRIS for Health's Bulk FHIR didn't work well for one site and another cited limited FHIR support.
quote: BulkFHIR feature didn't work very well for us

title: X12 and non-HL7 formats are second-class
summary: Qvera users want better X12 file support; InterSystems markets Mirth as lacking native CDA, DICOM, X12 and MQTT.

title: Native JSON Schema, YAML and XML-to-JSON handling
summary: Users requested native JSON Schema validation, Swagger-based payload validation, a YAML adaptor and dynamic XML-to-JSON conversion, plus fixing a buggy JSON-ignore-null parameter (21 votes).

title: Built-in de-identification of message data
summary: A Health Connect customer wants the engine to strip identifiers from data natively (e.g. for analytics or test feeds).
quote: capacity to remove the data identifiers

title: TLS/certificate management and MFA gated behind paid tiers
summary: SSL Manager, MFA and Command Center are enterprise-only; users complained years ago that paying for SSL management made the open-source edition near useless. Forks now advertise a free TLS plugin.

title: Separate tamper-resistant audit store
summary: InterSystems sells secure, separated audit storage and audit-ready logging as a differentiator against Mirth; Rhapsody markets audit-ready logging against Cloverleaf.

title: Secrets/vault integration for credentials
summary: Idea requesting secrets management via an external vault; delivered by a community package rather than the product.

title: UI papercuts: navigation, window handling, sorting
summary: Missing back/continue buttons, scattered functions, editor windows that open too small or one at a time, cluttered screens, slow-loading client, unsorted dropdowns and unlinked task pages.
quote: a long time for the Corepoint Integration Engine to load its interface

title: Consistent way to attach and query metadata on a message
summary: InterSystems users want a standard mechanism to store and fetch metadata with a message; a Mirth reviewer notes custom metadata columns carry a performance cost.

title: Generate REST clients, docs and tests from OpenAPI specs
summary: Several ideas: wizard to generate REST clients from OpenAPI, Swagger docs from REST services, unit tests from specs, ReDoc rendering, and VS Code REST debugger that reads OpenAPI.

title: Admin and security configuration should be scriptable via API
summary: Requests for a REST API over the security package, expect-style automation of routines, a read-only ops cockpit on management APIs, and an SDK for the integration platform.
quote: We would really love an SDK!

title: Product built for large enterprises; small customers neglected or priced out
summary: Rhapsody should consider different customer scales; smaller Cloverleaf customers struggle to get attention; IRIS pricing is too high at small scale; Redox is not well suited to small deployments.
quote: the price is too much at smaller scale

title: Confusing licensing models and contract friction
summary: Mirth customers face multiple licensing models, heavy finance coordination, and vendor licence terms that constrain building their own data feeds; a Redox customer was denied a refund despite no service delivered; Health Connect SKU lacks class-building available in IRIS.
quote: There are multiple licensing models with NextGen Healthcare.

title: Canonical data model doesn't fit real use cases
summary: Redox reviewers say its custom normalized models don't always match their workflow, complex legacy mappings still need configuration, and they wished for native FHIR instead.
quote: Custom data model, wish Redox supported FHIR natively

title: Message ordering not guaranteed across flows
summary: A Redox reviewer notes message order cannot be guaranteed across data models, a correctness risk for ADT/order sequences.

title: Integration network coverage limited to EHRs and supported workflows
summary: Interoperability is mostly limited to EHRs; specialised local routing, unusual protocols and deep hospital workflows are a poor fit; one customer said it failed to deliver the EHR integration.
quote: Redox failed to deliver EHR integration.

title: Engines turn vendors into custom-interface factories
summary: For digital-health vendors, every new customer needs its own VPN, feed, mapping and testing, accumulating permanent per-customer integration debt; reusable templates per EHR are the wish.

title: Running multiple engines because the EHR mandates its own
summary: Epic customers must run Bridges alongside their enterprise engine, so engine value is questioned; job postings expect skills in both Bridges and Cloverleaf.

title: Underlying infrastructure limits deter repurchase
summary: A Rhapsody manager would not buy again due to limitations in its underlying infrastructure; another expects to move off Rhapsody within a year.
quote: limitations in its underlying infrastructure

title: BizTalk is far more complex than it needs to be
summary: Reviewers attribute BizTalk's complexity to many degrees of freedom in wiring parts together, needing many separate tools to administer.
quote: far more complex than it needs to be

title: Business rules engine separate from code
summary: BizTalk's business rule engine is praised after a decade of use, and InterSystems' graphical rules/routing tools are a selling point; users want routing logic editable as rules rather than scripts. Note: praised in competitors.

title: Automatic load-based routing across servers
summary: BizTalk users praise how it redirects messages based on server load without intervention. Note: praised in competitor.

title: High throughput and rock-solid stability
summary: What buyers praise most in enterprise engines: Rhapsody 'super high throughput', Cloverleaf 'extremely stable and robust' on Linux, Health Connect runs reliably in the background with large volumes. Note: praised in competitors.
quote: Super high throughput and robust interface engine

title: Flexible Swiss-army-knife engine with low entry cost
summary: Mirth is praised as flexible, nimble, easy to pick up and cheap; Qvera users use it for workflows far beyond HL7. Users want that flexibility without losing enterprise features. Note: praised traits.

title: More control over integration than Mirth or Cloverleaf
summary: A verified AWS reviewer switched from Mirth and Cloverleaf to Rhapsody because it gave more control over the integration layer. Note: praised in competitor.

title: Interface timelines slip and vendors overstate integration capability
summary: KLAS finds customers frequently frustrated by integration timelines and vendors that misrepresent integration capabilities or go quiet when problems arise.
